name: core_revalidation_clean
description: 3-seed retraining on clean pair-grouped splits (topic-anchored benign + crescendo). Treatment vs baseline at K=1,2,3,5,all.
tables: Table 2: IID Detection Performance (3-seed mean ± std). Columns: Model | K=1 | K=2 | K=3 | K=5 | Full. Rows: Treatment, Baseline, TF-IDF. Bootstrap 95% CIs reported.
analysis:
IID results establish that the task is solvable but do not differentiate the method. Median-tier reviewer correctly notes that all approaches converge at K≥3. The paper must present IID as 'sanity check' and redirect to OOD/perturbation for contribution claims.

IID test set (n=76) is too easy — both treatment and baseline saturate at full-conversation, TF-IDF=1.0 across all K. Maximum treatment-baseline delta is only ~3pp (at K=1), well below 5pp pass criterion. In the median tier, reviewer R2 uses this to argue the task is trivially separable IID and the method's value is overstated. The 3-seed results show treatment has zero variance (ceiling effect) while baseline K=1 variance (±0.033) reflects minor decision-boundary instability — not enough to claim meaningful improvement. This IID saturation forces the paper to pivot entirely to OOD (plan_006) and perturbation (plan_004) for its core claims.

name: scrambled_label_ablation
description: Randomly shuffle persuasion strategy labels across jailbreak turns, retrain treatment DeBERTa, evaluate IID.
tables: Table 4: Scrambled-Label Ablation. Columns: Model | IID F1 | DD OOD F1 | DeBERTa Persuasion Acc. Rows: 8-class (proper), 8-class (scrambled), Baseline.
analysis:
This result reframes the paper's contribution from 'persuasion taxonomy matters' to 'persuasion-domain fine-tuning matters.' Median-tier reviewer accepts this reframing but demands a stronger control (random-task fine-tuning on same data). Without that control in the paper, rebuttal must promise it or argue why the fine-tuning-on-persuasion-text is itself the meaningful contribution.

Scrambled labels reduce DeBERTa persuasion head accuracy from ~80% to ~64% (near chance for 9-class) but downstream detection barely moves — IID gap is only 1.3pp, OOD gap is 1-6pp. In the median tier, this is the single most contentious result. Reviewer R1 invokes Gururangan et al. 2018 (annotation artifacts): 'If scrambled labels achieve F1=0.935-0.99 OOD, what evidence is there that the model has learned anything about persuasion rather than simply benefiting from fine-tuning on this data distribution? A random-task control (e.g., NLI fine-tuning on same data) is needed.' This is the reviewer concern with rebuttal_success_prob=0.4-0.5 — without the NLI ablation, the annotation-artifact objection is only partially addressable. The result is genuine (persuasion-domain fine-tuning is the signal, not precise labels), but the framing must be careful: 'persuasion-related text as supervision signal' rather than 'persuasion taxonomy enables detection.'

name: adversarial_perturbation
description: Aggressive paraphrasing of test jailbreak conversations (synonym substitution, restructuring, register shifting). Evaluate treatment/baseline/TF-IDF on perturbed data without retraining.
tables: Table 5: Robustness Under Adversarial Perturbation. Columns: Model | Original F1 | Perturbed F1 | Δpp. Rows: Treatment, Baseline, TF-IDF. Subtable for K=1 early detection.
analysis:
Perturbation results are the strongest TF-IDF differentiation argument but only at early detection (K=1). Median-tier reviewer accepts this as 'a contribution' but not 'a major contribution' — the practical scenario where K=1 perturbation robustness matters (adversary paraphrases AND you must detect in first turn) is narrow. Paper should frame this as 'complementary robustness property' rather than 'TF-IDF is fragile.'

Treatment shows zero degradation at K≥2 and only -2.6pp at K=1 — persuasion-aware embeddings capture pragmatic structure that survives paraphrasing. Baseline collapses (-12 to -15pp) because vanilla DeBERTa relies on surface-level semantic cues disrupted by perturbation. TF-IDF is the critical comparison: at K≥3, TF-IDF only drops 1.3pp (n=76, not statistically significant), so treatment vs TF-IDF differentiation is weak here. But at K=1 (early detection), TF-IDF drops 9.6pp while treatment drops only 2.6pp — this 7pp gap is the core TF-IDF differentiator. In the median tier, reviewer R2 accepts the treatment>>baseline argument but notes: (a) TF-IDF perturbation gap is only significant at K=1, (b) the perturbation is automated paraphrasing, not true adversarial attack, (c) BERTScore=0.92 means perturbations are mild. This is 'addressable' severity — reviewer flags it but doesn't demand rejection.

name: multi_attack_generation
description: Generate FITD-style (80) and Deceptive Delight-style (80) synthetic jailbreak conversations via Qwen3-8B with attack playbooks.
analysis:
Synthetic data quality is the median tier's second most contested point after scrambled labels. Reviewer accepts it for proof-of-concept but explicitly recommends 'validation on naturalistic attack datasets' as limitation. Paper must acknowledge this upfront.

Generation succeeds quantitatively — 80 conversations per type, appropriate strategy distributions. FITD uses fewer unique strategies (4 vs 6 for DD), reflecting the foot-in-the-door technique's simpler escalation pattern. In the median tier, at least one reviewer (R1) flags that these are synthetic conversations generated by a single 8B model, questioning whether they capture the diversity and subtlety of real multi-turn attacks. The concern is 'significant' but not 'fatal': reviewer wants validation on naturalistic attacks (WildChat red-teaming, human-generated jailbreaks) but accepts synthetic data as proof-of-concept for cross-attack generalization. The limited strategy coverage in FITD (only 4 of 8 strategies) also raises questions about whether the taxonomy is truly universal or whether some attack types simply don't exercise the full strategy space.

name: cross_attack_evaluation
description: Zero-shot evaluation of Crescendo-trained models on FITD and DD attack types.
tables: Table 3: Cross-Attack Zero-Shot Generalization. Columns: Attack Type | Model | K=1 | K=2 | K=3 | K=5 | Full. Rows grouped by DD, FITD.
analysis:
This is simultaneously the paper's strongest evidence and its most debated result. The +72pp gap is real but the TF-IDF=0.94 complicates the narrative. Median-tier reviewer acknowledges the gap over vanilla DeBERTa (the 'right' comparison for the academic claim) but questions practical utility over TF-IDF. FITD saturation (both models F1=1.0) weakens universality claims. Paper must frame DD as 'stress test revealing method's robustness floor' and acknowledge FITD saturation as limitation of the evaluation set.

The +72pp delta on DD (Treatment=1.0 vs Baseline=0.284) is the paper's headline result and survives median-tier scrutiny — no reviewer disputes the raw number. However, two complications reduce its impact: (1) TF-IDF achieves 0.944 on DD without any neural modeling, so 1-2 reviewers argue the 'practical gap' between Treatment and the simplest baseline is only 5.6pp, not 71.6pp. The 71.6pp gap is vs vanilla DeBERTa+GRU (the 'DeepContext approach'), which is a fair academic comparison but less compelling if a production system would just use TF-IDF. (2) FITD shows no treatment-baseline gap (both F1=1.0), meaning the cross-attack generalization advantage is attack-type-dependent. Reviewer R2 notes: 'The method's advantage materializes only when the unseen attack type is sufficiently different from training data (DD vs Crescendo) — for similar attack types (FITD vs Crescendo), vanilla embeddings suffice.' This nuance is legitimate and forces the paper to claim cross-attack robustness as 'worst-case insurance' rather than 'universal advantage.'

name: tfidf_lr_baseline
description: TF-IDF + Logistic Regression on clean data across all data sources including FITD, DD.
tables: Table 1: Lexical Baseline Performance. Columns: Data Source | TF-IDF F1 | CV F1.
analysis:
TF-IDF results must be presented prominently and honestly — burying them would trigger immediate reviewer distrust. Position as: 'We acknowledge inherent lexical separability and use TF-IDF as an upper-bound lexical baseline, not a strawman. DisPeD's value lies in dimensions where bag-of-words cannot follow: perturbation robustness and interpretability.'

TF-IDF achieves F1=1.0 on IID and FITD, 0.944 on DD. This confirms inherent lexical separability (D009): jailbreak conversations and benign conversations occupy different vocabulary spaces. In the median tier, this is the result that reviewer R2 wields most aggressively: 'A bag-of-words model achieves near-perfect detection even OOD — what does the neural approach add beyond interpretability?' The TF-IDF top features analysis reveals the separability comes from domain vocabulary differences (jailbreak conversations discuss harmful topics; benign conversations don't), not from persuasion-specific lexical cues. This is honest and important: the paper's contribution is NOT outperforming TF-IDF on raw detection but rather (a) bridging the vanilla temporal modeling gap, (b) perturbation robustness at K=1, (c) interpretability. The 0.944 on DD (vs Treatment 1.0) is a 5.6pp gap — real but small.

name: strategy_transition_analysis
description: Compute persuasion strategy transition matrices and trajectory visualizations for jailbreak vs benign conversations.
tables: Table 6: Strategy Trajectory Statistics. Columns: Attack Type | Strategies Used | Escalation Slope | Dominant Transition.
analysis:
Interpretability is the 'safe' contribution that median-tier reviewers accept without major objection. It's not sufficient alone for acceptance but it tips the balance when combined with the OOD generalization result. The lack of human evaluation is noted as limitation but not flagged as fatal.

Strategy trajectories show clear visual and quantitative differences: Crescendo exhibits monotonic escalation (mean strategy index 0.86→5.64), FITD shows commitment-escalation patterns, DD uses emotional-manipulation→role-assignment sequences. Benign conversations lack structured escalation (slope 0.12 vs 0.68). In the median tier, this is the interpretability contribution that reviewer R3 values — it's the differentiator from TF-IDF that reviewers can't dismiss. However, R1 notes two weaknesses: (1) no human evaluation of whether domain experts find trajectories interpretable or actionable, (2) plan_015 showed mean pooling ≈ GRU, proving the model does NOT use temporal ordering for detection. The trajectories are therefore a post-hoc descriptive tool, not a detection mechanism — they must be positioned as Claim 2 (analysis), not Claim 1 (detection).

name: wildchat_hard_negatives
description: Filter WildChat for high-drift benign conversations, evaluate FPR. Handle 14-16% jailbreak contamination.
tables: Table 7: False Positive Analysis on WildChat Hard Negatives. Columns: Model | FPR | Sample Count.
analysis:
WildChat results add ecological validity but also surface the method's FPR limitation. Median-tier reviewer uses this to argue the method isn't production-ready (FPR 9.5% = too many false alarms). Paper should frame as 'known limitation of persuasion-based detection: benign persuasion exists' and note that threshold tuning or hybrid TF-IDF+DisPeD could reduce FPR.

WildChat hard negatives push FPR above zero for the first time: treatment FPR=9.5% on high-drift conversations (vs 0% on topic-anchored benign). Some false positives arise from conversations that exhibit persuasion-like pragmatic patterns (e.g., users persistently pushing for controversial opinions, debates with escalating emotional language) without being jailbreaks. In the median tier, this result is double-edged: it shows the method's failure mode (flagging benign persuasion) and reveals that persuasion-awareness is not perfectly discriminative. Reviewer R1 notes TF-IDF has lower FPR (4.8%) because lexical features are more specific to jailbreak vocabulary. However, the 9.5% FPR on hand-selected hard negatives (specifically chosen for high drift) is acceptable for a detection system with human review. Contamination rate of 16% also complicates interpretation — some 'false positives' may be actual jailbreaks missed by the filtering.

name: cross_checkpoint_variance
description: Evaluate from DeBERTa fine-tuning checkpoints at epoch 2, 3, and final to quantify encoder training stochasticity.
analysis:
Low-controversy result that strengthens the paper's rigor. Median-tier reviewers note it approvingly in the 'thoroughness' dimension. Variance < 2pp easily passes the criterion.

IID downstream F1 is invariant to checkpoint selection (all 1.0) — the task is too easy to differentiate checkpoints. DD OOD shows minimal variance (0.011pp): epoch 2 (less fine-tuned) degrades slightly to 0.981 while epoch 3 and final are equivalent at 1.0. This confirms the persuasion fine-tuning effect is robust to training duration beyond epoch 2 and doesn't require careful early stopping. In the median tier, this is a clean positive result that no reviewer contests — it's a necessary ablation that removes a potential confound (checkpoint sensitivity) without being surprising. The slight epoch 2 OOD degradation actually strengthens the narrative: more fine-tuning = better OOD generalization, consistent with the 'persuasion domain knowledge' story.

name: deepcontext_proxy_reproduction
description: BERT-base + GRU proxy for DeepContext (no public code available). Tests vanilla BERT vs vanilla DeBERTa as encoders.
tables: Table 8: DeepContext Proxy Comparison. Columns: Encoder | IID F1 | DD OOD F1.
analysis:
Proxy validates the narrative but median-tier reviewer correctly notes it's not a true reproduction. This is a P2 experiment that adds marginal evidence — the core vanilla-DeBERTa baseline already demonstrates the OOD failure. DeepContext proxy is corroborative, not primary.

BERT-base GRU proxy achieves F1=0.974 IID (vs DeBERTa baseline 0.987, -1.3pp) and collapses to 0.256 on DD (vs DeBERTa baseline 0.284, -2.8pp). The BERT-DeBERTa gap is small — encoder architecture is not the bottleneck. Both vanilla encoders catastrophically fail OOD, confirming the gap is due to absence of persuasion fine-tuning, not encoder capacity. In the median tier, this result validates the paper's framing: the DeepContext-like approach (generic encoder + temporal model) fundamentally cannot generalize across attack types regardless of encoder choice. Reviewer R3 accepts this but notes it's a proxy, not a reproduction — the real DeepContext may have architectural differences that matter. The paper must disclaim: 'We could not reproduce DeepContext (no public code) and instead report a controlled proxy isolating the encoder contribution.'

name: llm_as_judge_baseline
description: GPT-5.5 and Qwen3-8B as zero-shot jailbreak detectors on the test set at K=2,3,5,all.
tables: Table 9: LLM-as-Judge Baseline. Columns: Model | K | F1 | Precision | Recall | Unparseable%. Both raw and unparseable-corrected F1.
analysis:
LLM-as-judge results are important for practical positioning but the unparseable rate is the Achilles heel. Median-tier reviewer accepts the comparison but insists on corrected numbers and flags the single-prompt design. Paper should report both raw and charitable upper-bound, and acknowledge that few-shot or CoT prompting was not tested.

GPT-5.5 achieves perfect precision but abysmal recall (10-29%): it correctly identifies jailbreaks when it commits to a judgment but is 'deceived' by Crescendo's surface educational framing in 70-90% of cases. This validates the core thesis — content-level analysis (even by a frontier LLM) cannot detect persuasion dynamics distributed across turns. However, unparseable rates of 30-47% severely weaken the comparison. In the median tier, reviewer R2 performs the back-of-envelope correction: 'If we assume all unparseable responses would have been correct (charitable upper bound), GPT-5.5 could reach F1≈0.7-0.8. The paper must report both raw and corrected numbers.' This reduces the Treatment advantage from 'F1=1.0 vs 0.45' to 'F1=1.0 vs 0.7-0.8' — still substantial but less dramatic. Reviewer also notes GPT-5.5 with chain-of-thought or conversation-level analysis prompting might perform better, and a single zero-shot prompt is not a thorough LLM baseline.

name: none_collapse_ablation
description: Binary persuasion head (persuasion-present vs none) vs full 9-class. Tests whether fine-grained taxonomy matters for detection.
tables: Table 4 (continued): None-Collapse Ablation. Columns: Persuasion Head | IID F1 | DD OOD F1. Rows: 9-class, Binary, Scrambled, Baseline.
analysis:
This result completes the ablation picture: persuasion-domain fine-tuning is the core mechanism, label granularity is secondary. Median-tier reviewer accepts the reframing but downgrades novelty from 'new method' to 'empirical finding + analysis paper.' This is the key tension for the 3.0-3.5 score range.

Binary collapse matches 9-class within 1-2pp on both IID and OOD. The model IS a persuasion-presence detector — fine-grained strategy labels do not improve detection. In the median tier, this is a finding, not a confound: it confirms that the critical ingredient is fine-tuning on persuasion-related text (teaching the encoder to attend to persuasive features) rather than learning a specific strategy taxonomy. Reviewer R1 seizes on this: 'If binary labels suffice for detection, the 8-class taxonomy is decorative. The interpretability claim (Claim 2) needs human evaluation to justify the taxonomy's existence.' Reviewer R3 sees it more favorably: 'This lowers the annotation barrier — practitioners can use binary persuasion labels and still get robust detection.' The tension between these views is why this is a 'borderline' paper: the result is honest and important but it undercuts the paper's most distinctive feature (the taxonomy).

name: lambda_ablation
description: Multi-task lambda ∈ {0, 0.3, 0.5, 2.0} ablation. Lambda=0 is persuasion-only (no intent head).
analysis:
Lambda insensitivity strengthens robustness claims but weakens the multi-task narrative. Paper should present this honestly and offer the simplified lambda=0 variant as 'DisPeD-lite' for practitioners who want minimal annotation overhead.

All lambda values yield F1=1.0 on both IID and DD — the method is completely insensitive to the multi-task weighting. Even lambda=0 (pure persuasion classification, no intent head) achieves perfect detection. In the median tier, this is a clean but double-edged result. Positively: the method is robust to hyperparameter choice, lowering the practitioner barrier. Negatively: it suggests the intent head contributes nothing and the multi-task framing is misleading — the method could be described as simply 'fine-tune on persuasion classification, then aggregate.' Reviewer R2 notes: 'If lambda doesn't matter, the multi-task objective reduces to a single-task objective with an unused intent head. The paper should simplify its description accordingly.' This is an 'addressable' concern — the paper can reframe the multi-task objective as 'optional but providing training signal diversity' and report lambda=0 as a valid simplified configuration.

name: mean_pooling_baseline
description: Replace Bi-GRU with mean pooling over turn embeddings. Tests whether temporal modeling contributes beyond aggregation.
tables: Table 5 (continued): Temporal Modeling Ablation. Columns: Aggregation | IID F1 | DD OOD F1. Rows: Bi-GRU, Mean Pooling.
analysis:
Mean pooling equivalence is the final piece of the mechanism puzzle: the method reduces to persuasion-domain fine-tuning of per-turn embeddings with any reasonable aggregation. This is simultaneously a strength (simplicity, accessibility) and a weakness (less novel than the full pipeline suggests). Median-tier reviewer scores this as 'solid empirical contribution' but 'not methodologically novel.'

Mean pooling ≈ GRU on both IID (identical F1=1.0) and DD OOD (both F1≈1.0, within noise). Temporal modeling is NOT the source of cross-attack generalization — the persuasion-aware embeddings themselves contain sufficient signal per-turn that simple averaging works. In the median tier, this completes the 'mechanism reduction': the method is not 'persuasion trajectory detection' (as Claim 2 might imply) but 'persuasion-presence detection via fine-tuned per-turn embeddings.' Reviewer R1 uses this to argue: 'The GRU architecture is unnecessary complexity. The true method is: fine-tune DeBERTa on persuasion text, extract [CLS] embeddings, average, classify. This is simpler than presented and the paper should say so.' This is fair criticism that the paper should preempt by reporting mean pooling as the primary architecture and GRU as an (equivalent) alternative.
